name: Survivorship bias
statement: Conclusions get drawn from the cases that made it far enough to be counted, and the cases that did not are missing from the data rather than absent from the world.
meaning: This is a property of a sample rather than a habit of a mind, which makes it unlike most entries here. The mechanism is selection: something has already filtered what you can observe, and the filter is correlated with the thing you are trying to measure. That makes this one species of selection bias, entry 82, the species in which the filter is survival. Berkson's paradox, entry 58, is the neighbouring species, in which the filter is admission. Studying successful companies tells you what successful companies have in common, including everything they share with the failed companies you never hear about. The error is not in the reasoning applied to the data; it is that the data arrived pre-sorted and nothing in it says so.

origin.where: the Statistical Research Group, Columbia University
origin.note: Wald's work is a series of eight memoranda written in 1943 for the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, under the National Defense Research Committee. The Center for Naval Analyses reprinted them in July 1980 as Research Contribution CRC 432, and the Defense Technical Information Center holds that reprint as ADA091073. Wald did not name the bias. The phrase survivorship bias appears nowhere in the reprint, and his contribution was a method for recovering the distribution you cannot see from the one you can. The reasoning is older. Francis Bacon's Novum Organum of 1620, book I aphorism XLVI, has a man shown votive tablets hung in a temple by those who escaped shipwreck, and pressed to acknowledge the power of the gods. His reply, in Joseph Devey's translation, is a question: 'But where are the portraits of those who have perished in spite of their vows?' Bacon files the story under the mind's preference for affirmatives over negatives, not under sampling.

evidence: The reprint's own abstract describes methods for estimating the vulnerability of various parts of an aircraft from damage to surviving planes. Armour appears once, at the end of the eighth memorandum, where Wald writes that the table of vulnerabilities and the other conclusions drawn from it "can be used as guides for locating protective armor and can be used to make a prediction of the estimated loss of a future mission". The aircraft is never called a bomber, and the worked example is explicitly a set of hypothetical data for a mission of 1,000 planes, of which 634 attacked the objective and 32 were lost. Wald also set out the limit the popular telling drops. Survivor damage alone cannot separate two explanations for an area with few recorded hits: that the area is rarely hit, and that hits there stop a plane returning. He assumed the distribution of hits across areas was known in advance, from the dispersion of the guns, or established by firing dummy bullets and recording where they struck. The finance literature supplies the measured examples. Elton, Gruber and Blake began from 361 funds listed as common stock in the 1977 Wiesenberger directory, which reports 1976 data. Returns were computed only for the 207 holding $15 million or more at the end of 1976, less 19 restricted funds, leaving 188; survival rates used all 361. They tracked those funds to December 1993 and defined bias as the average alpha of surviving funds minus the average alpha of all funds. Their Table 7, for a three-index model, gives the bias by assumed length of study. At 20 years the four estimates run from 0.896% to 1.108% a year, and at 10 years from 0.348% to 0.489%. Table 8 repeats the exercise for a one-index model, where the 20-year estimates run from 0.034% to 0.923%, and the authors say they do not consider the two no-reinvestment cases there appropriate.

replication.headline: Experiments on whether people discount a sample they know was selected find the neglect repeatedly, and disagree about whether telling people about the selection fixes it.
replication.detail: The structural claim has nothing to replicate. The cognitive claim next to it, that people read selected samples as though they were representative, has been tested and goes by the name selection neglect. Koehler and Mercer ran two experiments on a mutual fund advertisement. In their Study 2, 128 novice and 129 expert investors rated a fictitious company; mean willingness to invest, on a one to seven scale, was 4.7 for novices told the two advertised funds were the only two, 4.7 when the total was not stated, and 3.9 when they were told the funds were two of thirty. Expert means were 3.5, 3.6 and 2.9. Nine investors failed the manipulation check and were dropped. Study 3 recruited 180 business students and analysed 148 after exclusions. Barron, Huck and Jehiel report "strong evidence of selection neglect" in an investment game where players learn from others' outcomes. Where the papers part company is on transparency. Koehler and Mercer found the effect removed when the advertisement made the selection explicit. López-Pérez, Pintér and Sánchez-Mangas found no selection neglect in a lab treatment where subjects knew the exact selection rule, and neglect in two treatments where the rule was ambiguous. Van der Valk, Walker, Fugelsang and Koehler, on 640 United States residents across two experiments, report that disclosure is not enough: people told the sample was biased still overestimated partisan extremity, and were no less confident for it. Searches were run at Crossref by title and by query, at Europe PMC, at the OSF preprint index covering PsyArXiv, at the AEA registry of randomised trials, and through Google Scholar and general web search, under survivorship bias, selection neglect, sample selection and censored samples. No direct replication of any one of these protocols was found.

study.cite: Barron, K., Huck, S., & Jehiel, P. (2024). Everyday econometricians: selection neglect and overoptimism when learning from others. American Economic Journal: Microeconomics, 16(3), 162-198.

limits: Survivorship bias is a property of a sample rather than an effect measured on people, so the structural half of it is closer to a theorem than to a finding: given a filter correlated with the outcome, the surviving sample is biased, and that follows rather than being tested. The experiments above test the other half, whether people allow for the filter, and they run on urns, advertisements and investment games rather than on the historical cases the label is usually applied to. Brundage, Little and You make that gap the complaint of their review, writing that much empirical research is consistent with selection neglect but rarely tests the mechanism directly outside the lab. What can be measured in the field is the size of the distortion in a particular dataset, and Elton, Gruber and Blake did that for one set of American mutual funds over one period. The label gets applied well past the cases where anyone has quantified anything, and its usefulness there rests on the argument rather than on evidence.
misreadings: The bomber diagram that circulates with this story is a modern illustration. Its Wikimedia Commons description calls Wald's 1943 report unillustrated and records the picture as McGeddon's 2016 drawing, based on a Lockheed PV-1 Ventura and on US Air Force hit plots of the kind published in 1991, vectorised by Martin Grandjean in 2021. The reprint's text was read for this entry and carries equations and tables of vulnerabilities rather than plane diagrams. The story is also often told as though Wald reversed a decision the military had already made. Mangel and Samaniego, who condensed the memoranda for the Journal of the American Statistical Association, write in their rejoinder that they do not know whether the work was used during the Second World War, while recording its later use on the A-4 in Vietnam and on the B-52 at Wright Patterson Air Force Base. The larger misuse is rhetorical: pointing out that a sample survived something is not by itself an argument that its lesson is wrong, only that the missing cases have to be reasoned about. Used as a conversational trump card it explains every success story equally well, which is another way of saying it explains none of them.

sources.text: Wald, A. (1943). A method of estimating plane vulnerability based on damage of survivors. Eight memoranda for the Statistical Research Group, Columbia University; reprinted July 1980 by the Center for Naval Analyses as Research Contribution CRC 432, held by the Defense Technical Information Center as ADA091073, which returned HTTP 403 to this search. Read for this entry from a copy of CRC 432 bound together with the Mangel and Samaniego article, the published comments on it, and the authors' rejoinder. The scan carries no text layer for its figures, so the claim that the report is unillustrated is taken from the Wikimedia Commons description below rather than asserted here.

Mangel, M., & Samaniego, F. J. (1984). Abraham Wald's work on aircraft survivability. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(386), 259-267, with comments and the authors' rejoinder at 267-271.

Elton, E. J., Gruber, M. J., & Blake, C. R. (1996). Survivorship bias and mutual fund performance. The Review of Financial Studies, 9(4), 1097-1120. Tables 1, 7 and 8 give the sample and the bias estimates quoted here. The printed article title is Survivorship Bias and Mutual Fund Performance; Crossref and Oxford Academic index it as Survivor Bias and Mutual Fund Performance. Read from a JSTOR scan with no text layer, so every figure above was taken from an optical character recognition pass and checked against the surrounding prose, which restates the 20-year range of 1.108% and 0.896%.

Koehler, J. J., & Mercer, M. (2009). Selection neglect in mutual fund advertisements. Management Science, 55(7), 1107-1121. Read in full from the author copy in the Northwestern University School of Law repository, which reproduces the published typesetting.

Barron, K., Huck, S., & Jehiel, P. (2024). Everyday econometricians: selection neglect and overoptimism when learning from others. American Economic Journal: Microeconomics, 16(3), 162-198. The published full text could not be obtained; the quoted phrase is from the abstract, which was read at Crossref and at the American Economic Association's article page. No figure from this paper is used above.

López-Pérez, R., Pintér, A., & Sánchez-Mangas, R. (2022). Some conditions (not) affecting selection neglect: evidence from the lab. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 195, 140-157. The published version sits behind Elsevier and returned HTTP 403; the treatment structure and the null under a known selection rule were read in the 2020 CSIC working paper of the same title, and no figure from it is used above.

van der Valk, A. M., Walker, A. C., Fugelsang, J. A., & Koehler, D. J. (2025). Disclosing sample bias fails to fully correct judgments of partisan extremity. Cognition, 256, 106050. The count of 640 participants across two experiments is from the abstract, read twice at Europe PMC; the full text was not obtained.

Brundage, J., Little, A. T., & You, S. (2024). Selection neglect and political beliefs. Annual Review of Political Science, 27(1), 63-85. The remark about direct tests outside the lab is from the abstract, read at Crossref.

Bacon, F. Novum Organum, edited by Joseph Devey (New York: P. F. Collier & Son, 1902). Book I aphorism XLVI, read as HTML at Project Gutenberg. The Latin was not consulted, and other translations word the votive-tablets reply differently.
